Title: [Excerpt from] Grandmother Five Baskets
Author: by Lisa Larrabee
Content: “Yes, little `text(one)`. We begin today,” Grandmother `text(Five)` Baskets had answered `text(twenty years)` ago to my insistent questions.
I ran to gather her shawl and basket as she pulled herself from the rocking chair. Though nearly `text(eighty)`, she moved gracefully as she stepped from the porch.
She told me what I should look for, as we walked along the rutted red road toward the stand of loblolly pine trees where she always collected the pine needles for her baskets.
“Anna, this is a good time to gather the pine straw, since there was a heavy rain several nights ago. The freshest straw will be lying on top of the old, and we need only to pick it up,” she said.
As we entered the cool darkness, the sunlight filtered through the pine trees. The light showed ferns and flowers pressing up through layers of leaves and pine straw...

Grandmother `text(Five)` Baskets moved slowly through the woods, stopping now and again, `text(each time)` calling me back to look at `text(one)` plant or another, and telling me its name and use. My favorite was a small bed of spearmint. The smell of the leaves was sweet and clean when crushed between my fingers. Grandmother `text(Five)` Baskets said she would use the leaves to make a tea to soothe upset stomachs or in a salve¹ to cool irritated skin. The afternoon passed for a pleasant `text(hour)` or so, until we had gathered enough pine straw for several baskets.

Our shadows showed the way, as we walked back to her house. While the sun began its nightly journey, Grandmother `text(Five)` Baskets told me that to learn the lessons of the `text(five)` baskets would require much from me.

“Little `text(one)`, you will find yourself tested now that you have decided to learn these lessons. And you will be learning more than just basketmaking. What your lessons will be, I cannot say. Some lessons are special to the person doing the learning. You will share problems others before you have had, but `text(one)` or `text(two)` of the problems you will discover are yours alone. While I will help as much as I am able, you will be the `text(one)` who must finally help yourself,” she said...

Grandmother `text(Five)` Baskets was not my actual grandmother. In fact, she was no one’s grandmother, as she had never married nor had children. She was my great-aunt, my grandmother’s sister. Her name was Sarah McGhee. Yet, in our small Creek Indian community of Hog Fork, Alabama, there were few people old enough to remember her by any name but Grandmother `text(Five)` Bask...

Her name, Grandmother `text(Five)` Baskets, was not earned for her helping ways. It was for her skill in basketmaking and the lessons of the `text(five)` baskets. These were seen, by those not having studied with her, as simple lessons in basketmaking. Yet, as any woman who completed her baskets learned, the lessons were much more. It was with deep love and respect that these women called her Grandmother `text(Five)` Baskets.

Of the lessons in basketmaking, not every girl in the community wanted to learn them nor finished once they had begun. Girls were most often `12` or `text(13 years)` old when they began to study with Grandmother Five Baskets. Yet, from time to time, women as old as `20` or more studied with her.

Listening to all the talk among my womenfolk from the time I was small made me eager for my chance to begin the lessons. Yet, it wasn’t the stories I heard that made the lessons appear special. It was the way the girls changed when they had completed their `text(five)` baskets. It was as if they gained a maturity or an inward serenity.² I wasn’t sure anyone else noticed, but I had. Whatever they received during those lessons, I wanted it, too. Now, in the summer of my `text(twelfth year)`, my chance was finally here.

During the next few `text(days)`, Grandmother `text(Five)` Baskets showed me how to clean the pine straw we had collected in warm, soapy water. I learned to rinse it well, and dry it carefully on old window screens laid on rocks in the sun. The screens allowed air to circulate completely around the pine straw and keep it from molding. I found reasons every `text(day)` to stop by her house and check on its progress. After several `text(days)` of drying in the warm sun, the pine straw was pronounced ready to use by Grandmother `text(Five)` Baskets...

I gathered my `text(first)` small bundle of straw and my needle with straw binder, and I began to coil and sew. I struggled to keep my coils even as I worked. My tongue pinched between my teeth was as hard to handle as the needle and pine straw between my fingers.

Finally, there stood a completed basket, a little lopsided, but mine. Though it was only a few `text(hours)` since I had begun the basket, it felt like `text(years)`. I was tired and very pleased with myself. I had made my `text(first)` basket. I could see that basketmaking wasn’t going to be hard at all!

“You have done well for your `text(first)` basket, little `text(one)`. When you come again, we will go gather the materials for your `text(second)`. Do not judge this `text(first)` basket too harshly, for your skills will improve with `text(each one)` you complete.”
References: salve: a creamy mixture to help the skin
